question: Ancient Egyptian embalmers went to enormous effort to preserve a body for the afterlife, yet they pulled the brain out through the nose and discarded it, while taking great care to leave the heart in place. Why the opposite treatment for these two organs?
correct_answer: Heart held thought and soul, brain didn't
alternative_answers: The heart was the seat of the mind and soul
The heart was needed for the weighing of the heart judgment
They thought the heart did the thinking, not the brain
The brain was considered useless; the heart held the person's essence
The heart was judged in the afterlife, the brain had no purpose
headline_answer: Heart held thought and soul, brain didn't

extra.verification_notes: Standard, well-sourced explanation: the ib/heart was held to be the seat of thought, emotion and moral character and was needed for the weighing-of-the-heart judgment, while the brain was thought functionless and discarded (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_funerary_practices); variability in excerebration across periods is a nuance, not a contradiction.

explanation: The Egyptians believed the heart, not the brain, was the seat of intelligence, memory and emotion, and therefore the essence of the person. It also had to be present for the judgment of the dead, when the heart was weighed against the feather of Maat to decide whether the deceased could enter the afterlife. The brain was regarded as unimportant, possibly just a producer of mucus, so it was removed and thrown away, while the heart was left in the chest and often protected with a heart scarab amulet.

question: What happened first: the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza, or the death of the last woolly mammoths?

extra.why_interesting: People picture mammoths as Ice Age creatures and pyramids as 'history', so learning they overlapped is a genuine shock.
extra.verification_notes: The Great Pyramid dates to c. 2600 BC (~4,600 BP) while the last woolly mammoths on Wrangel Island survived until ~4,000 BP (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth), a gap reaffirmed by the 2024 Cell genome study.

explanation: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC. A dwarf population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 2000 BC, so the pyramid stood for roughly five centuries while mammoths still walked the Earth.

question: Roman harbour concrete has survived 2,000 years of pounding waves and actually grows stronger with age. What volcanic ingredient did the Romans mix into it?

extra.why_interesting: Modern concrete crumbles in decades, yet Roman harbour walls are still standing and getting stronger. The player can reason backward from 'Italy, volcanoes, Vesuvius'.
extra.verification_notes: Roman marine concrete used volcanic ash (pozzolana) with lime and seawater, and the 2017 American Mineralogist research confirms seawater reacting with the ash grows aluminous tobermorite that strengthens it over time; the 2023 quicklime hot-mixing findings supplement rather than supersede this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_concrete).

explanation: The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash, known as pozzolana, from around the Bay of Naples. When seawater seeps in, it reacts with the ash to grow new crystals that seal cracks, so the concrete keeps healing itself.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for how long: closer to 400 years, 1,400 years, or 3,800 years?

extra.why_interesting: The correct option is the most extreme one, and the player can reason about when tall cathedrals appeared in Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives 'more than 3,700 years' (surpassed mid-13th c. by Old St Paul's) and elsewhere Lincoln Cathedral in 1311 (~3,870 years); both land far closer to 3,800 than to the other options — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

explanation: Completed around 2560 BC at about 146 metres, the pyramid was only overtaken around AD 1311 by the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England. That is a record of nearly 3,800 years that no building is likely to match.

question: Ancient Romans collected a certain liquid in public jars and used it to whiten togas and even to clean their teeth. What was it?

extra.why_interesting: Gross, funny and true. The chemistry (ammonia) gives a reasoning path for anyone who thinks about what a public jar might collect.
extra.verification_notes: Core claim is well attested (Vespasian's vectigal urinae; fullers used stale urine to whiten togas per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecunia_non_olet); only the decorative 'clean their teeth' clause is shaky, since ancient sources attribute that to Celtiberians rather than Romans, which does not affect the unique answer.

explanation: Stale urine breaks down into ammonia, a natural bleach and cleaner. Laundries left jars on street corners for passers-by, and Emperor Vespasian even taxed the trade in it.

question: One of these ancient civilisations never used the wheel for transport. Which one?

extra.why_interesting: All four are famous empire-builders, so the odd one is not visible on the surface. The player can deduce it by recalling that the Americas had no horses or oxen before Europeans arrived.
extra.verification_notes: Inca use of the wheel for transport is correctly ruled out (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system) and nothing newer contradicts it; caveat: the option list was not supplied, and the answer is only unique if Aztec/Maya are not among the distractors, since they also lacked wheeled transport (https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/home/the-concept-of-the-wheel-in-ancient-mesoamerica).

explanation: The Inca built some 40,000 kilometres of roads across the Andes, yet moved everything on foot or by llama. With no horses or oxen to pull carts, and steep mountain paths full of steps, the wheel offered them no advantage. Wheels appear only on a few children's toys in the Americas.

question: In the original ancient Greek Olympics, what did the athletes wear while competing?

extra.why_interesting: Recontextualises the most famous sporting event in the world; the answer is easy once you think of Greek statues.
extra.verification_notes: Athletes competing nude is well attested as the ancient Olympic norm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Olympic_Games); the pre-720 BC loincloth and the armoured hoplitodromos/clothed charioteers are minor caveats that don't yield a competing intended answer.

explanation: Athletes competed completely naked, coated in olive oil. The Greek word 'gymnasium' literally comes from 'gymnos', meaning naked. Married women were banned from even watching.

question: Ancient Egyptians mummified one household pet by the millions, even breeding them on temple farms just for that purpose. Name the animal.

extra.why_interesting: Mummification is famous for pharaohs; learning it was done industrially to a household pet is startling.
extra.verification_notes: Cat mummification by the millions with temple breeding is well documented (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cats_in_ancient_Egypt); minor caveat is that dogs (~7.8M mummies from 'puppy farms' at the Catacombs of Anubis, https://www.livescience.com/51232-millions-of-dog-mummies-found.html) also fit the wording loosely.

explanation: Cats were sacred to the goddess Bastet, and pilgrims bought mummified cats as offerings. So many were made that in the 19th century a shipment of about 180,000 cat mummies was sent to England and ground up as fertiliser.

question: In 1901, divers off a Greek island recovered a corroded bronze device packed with interlocking gears, now believed to have predicted eclipses. It is often called the world's first what?

extra.why_interesting: A 2,000-year-old geared machine that predicted eclipses breaks everyone's assumption about ancient technology. The story of the divers and the corroded bronze gives a reasoning path toward 'a machine that calculates'.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the mechanism was retrieved in July 1901 off Antikythera by sponge divers, contains interlocking bronze gears, predicted eclipses decades ahead, and is 'generally referred to as the first known analogue computer'; no older rival device and the 2025 jamming study does not overturn the designation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism)

explanation: The Antikythera mechanism, built around 100 BC, used dozens of bronze gears to model the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets and to forecast eclipses. Nothing of comparable complexity appears again until European clockwork more than a thousand years later.
